summary:
Ignis AI is a web app that turns NASA's microgravity combustion data into fire-safety insight. It has two parts, both built only on NASA data.


Predictive Lab: a machine-learning model trained on 52 real ISS flame tests (NASA BASS-II, PMMA rods) predicts how fast a flame spreads (mm/s) from oxygen level, airflow and rod diameter. Each result comes with an error range, a confidence level, warnings when inputs fall outside the tested range, and NASA's observed findings. Validation holds out whole physical samples, so it never tests on data it has seen.


Ask the Data: a chatbot built on retrieval-augmented generation answers questions from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics repository and the pages and PDFs linked from the challenge.


This addresses the challenge by making scattered microgravity combustion results searchable and usable for spacecraft fire safety. Fire is among the most dangerous risks in space, and flames behave differently without gravity.
details:
What it Does and How it Works

Ignis AI is a web app with two tools built on NASA data.

- Predictive Lab: a machine-learning model trained on 52 real ISS flame tests (NASA BASS-II, cast PMMA rods, from Link et al. 2018) predicts flame spread rate (mm/s) from oxygen %, airflow speed and rod diameter. Each result comes with an error range, a confidence level, warnings when inputs fall outside the tested range, and NASA's observed findings on the scenario.

- Ask the Data: a chatbot built on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). On setup the app pulls NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics records through their public JSON search endpoint. It also reads the Resources tab of the challenge page, follows the NASA links on it one level deeper, and reads PDFs such as the experiment fact sheets. Questions are matched to the best passages, and Claude writes an answer in Markdown with [PSI-xx] citations.

Benefits

- Microgravity fire research is spread across repositories, PDFs and papers. This puts it behind one search box.

- The predictor lets a person explore how oxygen and airflow change flame spread without reading raw tables.

- Every number and answer is traceable to a NASA source.

Intended Impact

Help engineers, students and researchers quickly understand spacecraft fire behavior, and show that a small public dataset can support honest, explainable AI. The design is meant to grow as more data, such as partial-gravity results from NASA's FM2 experiment, becomes available.

Tools and Technologies

- Python (FastAPI, uvicorn, scikit-learn, Pandas. NumPy, MatPlotLib)

- JavaScript (Vite.js, React)

- Anthropic Claude API

- NASA Data (NASA PSI, the Resources-tab pages and PDFs, and Link et al. (2018), Sci. Rep. 8:120, CC BY 4.0.)

- Other: a bash script (dev.sh), installs and runs everything. We worked on standard laptops, with no special hardware.

What our Team Considered

- Small data: with only 19 physical samples, we held out whole samples when validating so the scores aren't inflated, and we compared against a "predict the average" baseline.

- Reliability and security: the saved model retrains itself if the library version differs, and API keys stay out of the repository.
